q: Where does Methylospira mobilis Shm1 sit phylogenomically within Type-I methanotrophs (Methylococcaceae) once whole-proteome / core-genome trees are built, rather than the 16S-only placement in Oshkin et al. 2019?
basis: The paper (and our replication) only anchors Shm1↔Methylococcus capsulatus Bath at 16S rRNA identity 94.06% (paper) / 93.89% (ours). 16S identity at this level places the two organisms in the same family but is not enough to establish sister-group vs. deep-branch position within Methylococcaceae, nor to test whether spiral-shaped micro-aerobic methanotrophs form a monophyletic clade distinct from the classical Methylococcus/Methylomonas/Methylobacter radiation. A concatenated-marker or whole-proteome tree with all sequenced Type-I methanotrophs was outside our replication scope.
next_steps: Retrieve all publicly available complete Methylococcaceae genomes from NCBI (Methylococcus, Methylomonas, Methylobacter, Methylomicrobium, Methylosarcina, Methylocaldum, Methylovulum, Methylotuvimicrobium, plus other Methylospira draft genomes if any). Extract a bacterial single-copy core gene set (e.g. GTDB bac120 markers or Bacteria_odb10 BUSCOs) with hmmsearch, align each marker with mafft --auto, trim with trimAl -automated1, concatenate, and infer an IQ-TREE 2 phylogeny under LG+C60+F+G with 1000 ultrafast bootstraps. Report Shm1's sister taxon, its stem-branch length relative to Bath, and whether other spiral-shape methanotrophs (if genomes exist) cluster together.

q: Do Shm1's two pMMO clusters and single sMMO cluster show the canonical copper-switch regulatory architecture (Cu-responsive MmoR/MmoG + σ54 promoter upstream of mmoX), or is the regulatory logic remodeled relative to Methylococcus capsulatus Bath?
basis: REPORT.md confirms ≥2 pmoC subunit sets and the sMMO cluster at F6R98_10895–10905 with mmoD, and confirms MxaFI + XoxF methanol-DH presence. But our gene-presence work is annotation-substring-based; we did not test whether the pmoCAB1 vs. pmoCAB2 promoter regions carry distinct copper-responsive elements, whether MmoR/MmoG homologs are present upstream of mmoX with the canonical σ54 -12/-24 box, or whether Shm1 encodes the methanobactin biosynthesis cluster (mbnABC) known to modulate the copper switch in Bath. The paper reports the clusters' presence but not their regulatory architecture in detail.
next_steps: Extract 5 kb of upstream sequence for pmoCAB1, pmoCAB2, and mmoXYBZDC from CP044205. Scan for σ54 (-12 GC / -24 GG) promoter boxes with a PWM (e.g. Studholme–Dixon sigma54 model). Run HMMER against Pfam PF04068 (MmoR-like GAF) + PF00196 (LuxR C-terminal HTH) to identify Cu-responsive regulators. BLAST for mbnA (short cysteine-rich precursor) and mbnBC biosynthesis machinery. Additionally, an RNA-Seq experiment across a copper gradient (0.1 → 10 μM CuSO4) in an axenic Shm1 culture would directly test the switch — but that requires wet-lab access to strain Shm1 (VKM B-3350 / KCTC 15564).

q: What is the genetic basis of Shm1's characteristic spiral cell morphology and its high motility, and are the specific determinants (e.g. cytoskeletal ccrp/crescentin homologs, MreB modifications, curvature-generating peptidoglycan hydrolases) encoded in a discoverable cluster or dispersed?
basis: REPORT.md confirms 44 flagellar CDS with the full fli*/flg*/motAB set and a 35× expansion of chemotaxis CDS (52 vs. 2 in Bath), which explains motility. It does NOT address WHY the cells are spiral. Spiral morphology in bacteria has multiple known genetic bases (Helicobacter uses ccmA + CsdA/B peptidoglycan endopeptidases; Spiroplasma uses fibril MreB5; Caulobacter uses crescentin/CreS) and it is unknown which — if any — of these systems Methylospira uses. This is arguably the most biologically interesting question about the organism and it is completely untouched by the replication.
next_steps: HMMsearch CP044205 against Pfam models PF06276 (crescentin/CreS coiled-coil), PF16357 (CsdA peptidoglycan endopeptidase), PF06725 (CcmA membrane-anchor family), and the MreB family (PF06723) with subfamily-specific thresholds. Also BLAST the Shm1 proteome against the curated 'shape determinant' proteomes of Helicobacter pylori 26695, Vibrio cholerae O395, and Caulobacter crescentus CB15. Report any hits with e-value < 1e-20 and inspect gene neighborhoods for co-clustered peptidoglycan hydrolases. If nothing hits, this suggests a novel spiral-shape mechanism worth follow-up structural / genetic work.

q: Is Shm1's C1 assimilation architecture a complete RuMP cycle plus a partial serine cycle plus a partial CBB cycle (as the paper claims), or is one of the three pathways functionally complete enough to be a primary route — i.e., is Shm1 an obligate RuMP methanotroph, a facultative serine-cycle user, or a mixotroph?
basis: REPORT.md notes the paper's claim that Shm1 shares Bath's C1 metabolic core (pMMO + sMMO + MxaFI/XoxF MDH + RuMP + partial serine/CBB) and confirms PEP carboxylase presence in Shm1 (Bath absent), which is one signature of an operational serine-cycle anaplerotic node. But 'partial serine' and 'partial CBB' are qualitative labels — we did not enumerate WHICH serine-cycle genes are missing (glyA, sgaA, hprA, mtdA, mtdB, mch, fhs, gck, ppc, mcl, mtkAB, mclA) or which CBB genes are missing (rbcL, rbcS, prkB). Whether either pathway is functionally closed determines whether Shm1 can grow on non-methane C1 substrates.
next_steps: Build a curated HMM set for RuMP (hxlA, hxlB, phi, tal, tkt, rpe, rpi, fbaA, fbp, pfkA), serine cycle (glyA, sgaA, hprA, mtdA, mtdB, mch, fhs, gck, ppc, mcl, mtkAB, mclA), and CBB (rbcL, rbcS, cbbP/prkB, cbbT, cbbF) genes. Score CP044205 CDS with hmmsearch --cut_ga and record hit/miss for each pathway step. Report path completeness as a fraction and highlight any gaps that would break the cycle. Cross-check against the KEGG methanotrophy modules M00344 (RuMP), M00346 (serine), M00165 (CBB) via KAAS or eggNOG-mapper. A truly complete serine cycle would make Shm1 a much more metabolically flexible organism than the paper suggests.

q: Which gene families in Shm1 constitute a genomic signature for the specific water-saturated, micro-oxic, nitrogen-poor northern wetland habitat, and can this signature be validated by comparison against methanotroph genomes isolated from other habitats (rice paddies, deep aquifers, lake sediments, forest soils)?
basis: The paper interprets V-Fe nitrogenase, expanded chemotaxis/flagellar apparatus, dual bd + cbb3 oxidases, and heavy IS load as adaptations to wetland micro-oxic N-poor life. REPORT.md confirms all four gene-inventory features. But 'adaptation to wetlands' is an inference, not a demonstration: we did not compare Shm1's gene content against a habitat-stratified panel of other methanotroph genomes to test whether these features are ENRICHED in wetland isolates specifically vs. Type-I methanotrophs from other environments. Without a comparative panel, the adaptation story is plausible but not statistically supported.
next_steps: Curate a panel of ~30 methanotroph genomes stratified by isolation source (wetland/peat, rice paddy, lake sediment, deep aquifer, forest soil, marine, activated sludge) using GOLD / BioSample metadata. Build orthogroups with OrthoFinder or PPanGGOLiN. For each of the four candidate adaptation signatures (V-Fe nitrogenase presence, chemotaxis-CDS count, bd-oxidase copy number, IS-element load per Mbp), test enrichment in wetland isolates vs. others with a Fisher exact test (presence/absence) or Mann–Whitney U (count-based), controlling for genome size and multiple testing (BH-FDR). Report which — if any — of the paper's adaptation features are statistically over-represented in wetland methanotroph genomes. This turns the paper's narrative into a testable ecological-genomics hypothesis.
